title: Flask
summary: Flask is a small Python web framework: a developer registers view functions on an application object, and a WSGI server hands each HTTP request to it. For every request Flask pushes a context, runs the matching view, turns its return value into a response, and tears the context down again.

nodes.label: App developer
nodes.summary: Writes an application: creates the Flask object, registers routes and blueprints, and sets config.

nodes.label: WSGI server
nodes.summary: Werkzeug's dev server or a production server (Gunicorn, uWSGI) that calls the app once per request.
nodes.details: Flask itself never listens on a socket. `app.run()` and `flask run` start Werkzeug's development server; production deployments point any WSGI server at the app object.

nodes.label: Application object
nodes.summary: The Flask class: holds routes, blueprints, config, and hooks, and is the WSGI callable a server invokes.
nodes.details:
- `Flask` (app.py) adds the request-handling half on top of `App` (sansio/app.py), which has no I/O so other frameworks such as Quart can reuse it.
- `Scaffold` is the shared base for apps and blueprints: route decorators, before/after hooks, error handlers.
- Blueprints record their setup and replay it when registered on an app.
- `Config` is a dict with loaders for files, objects, and environment variables.

nodes.label: Flask class
nodes.summary: The public Flask object: sets up the app, exposes run() and test_client(), and is the WSGI callable a server invokes.
nodes.details:
- `Flask(__name__)` works out the app's root path for templates and static files.
- Adds the I/O-aware pieces on top of the shared `App` base: `run()` (starts Werkzeug's dev server), `test_client()`, `wsgi_app`/`__call__`.
- Re-exported from `flask/__init__.py` as the thing a developer imports.

nodes.label: Request dispatch
nodes.summary: The per-request pipeline: preprocess, match and call the view, handle any exception, finalize the response.
nodes.details:
- `full_dispatch_request` runs before_request hooks, then `dispatch_request` calls the matched view.
- Exceptions go through `handle_user_exception`, which looks up a registered error handler before falling back to a generic 500 in `handle_exception`.
- `finalize_request`/`make_response` turn the view's return value into a real Response object.

nodes.label: App + Scaffold base
nodes.summary: The I/O-free foundation Flask extends: the URL map, config, and the lists of hooks and error handlers.
nodes.details:
- `sansio/app.py`'s `App` holds the Werkzeug `Map`, the `Config` instance, and app-level hook/error-handler storage.
- `sansio/scaffold.py`'s `Scaffold` is shared by both `App` and `Blueprint`: `route`, `add_url_rule`, `before_request`, `after_request`, `teardown_request`, `errorhandler`.
- Has no socket or WSGI code, so other frameworks (the README names Quart) can reuse it.

nodes.label: Blueprint
nodes.summary: Records routes and hooks under a name/prefix, then replays them onto an app when registered.
nodes.details:
- `sansio/blueprints.py`'s `Blueprint` (itself a `Scaffold`) queues up `route`/`before_request`/etc. calls instead of applying them immediately.
- `register()` (via `BlueprintSetupState`) replays each queued call onto the app, with the blueprint's url_prefix and name applied.
- `flask/blueprints.py`'s `Blueprint` just adds the I/O-aware pieces back on top of the sansio version, mirroring the Flask/App split.

nodes.label: Config
nodes.summary: A dict subclass holding app settings, with loaders for Python objects, files, and environment variables.
nodes.details:
- `from_object`, `from_pyfile`, `from_envvar`, `from_prefixed_env`, `from_mapping` are the ways a developer feeds in settings.
- Created once per app and hung on `App.config`; read by both core Flask code and extensions.

nodes.label: Class-based views
nodes.summary: View and MethodView: lets a developer write a request handler as a class instead of a function.
nodes.details:
- `View.as_view()` wraps a class into the plain view function `add_url_rule` expects.
- `MethodView` dispatches to a same-named method (`get`, `post`, ...) based on the request method.

flows.name: What happens when the developer builds the app
flows.summary: Setup code that runs once, before any request arrives.

steps.text: Flask(__name__) creates the app and works out its template/static root paths.
The constructor sets up Config, the URL map, and the hook/error-handler lists on the shared base.
Class-based views are turned into plain view functions with View.as_view().
add_url_rule registers the resulting view function and endpoint on the app's URL map.
When the blueprint is registered, it replays every route and hook it had queued onto the app.

flows.name: What happens inside the app object for one request
flows.summary: The dispatch path from the WSGI call to a finished response.

steps.text: __call__ delegates to wsgi_app with the WSGI environ.
wsgi_app pushes a request context, then calls full_dispatch_request.
before_request hooks run, the URL is matched, and the matched view function is called.
Matching and hook order come from the Rule map and hook lists App/Scaffold maintain.
The view's return value is turned into a Response (a rendered template or JSON).
after_request hooks run, the session is saved, and the context is popped.

flows.name: What happens when a view raises
flows.summary: How an exception inside a view becomes a response.

steps.text: full_dispatch_request catches the exception and calls handle_user_exception.
handle_user_exception looks up a registered error handler by exception type, checking the blueprint's handlers before the app's.
If nothing matches, handle_exception converts an unhandled exception into a generic 500 response.

nodes.label: Request contexts
nodes.summary: Pushes a context per request so `request`, `session`, `g`, and `current_app` work, then tears it down.
nodes.details:
- In this version one `AppContext` carries both app and request state; `request_context()` returns an AppContext.
- `globals.py` exposes context-local proxies backed by a `ContextVar`.
- Sessions load from and save to a signed cookie by default (`SecureCookieSessionInterface`).
- Signals (Blinker) fire at request start, finish, teardown, and on exceptions.

nodes.label: Context push/pop
nodes.summary: Pushes an AppContext per request or CLI command, opens the session, matches the route, and tears down on pop.
nodes.details:
- Owns the active app, request, session, and g for the duration of a context.
- push() sets a contextvar, opens the session, then matches the URL against the app's routes.
- pop() runs teardown_request and teardown_appcontext functions, saves the session, then clears the contextvar.
- Supports nested pushes (a push count) so streaming or testing can re-enter without double teardown.
- after_this_request() registers a cleanup callback for just the current request.
- copy_current_request_context() lets a background task run inside a copy of the request context that spawned it.

nodes.label: Context proxies
nodes.summary: The request, session, g, current_app, and app_ctx objects imported everywhere, as thin proxies to the active context.
nodes.details:
- Each proxy is a Werkzeug LocalProxy bound to one ContextVar holding the current AppContext.
- Raises a clear RuntimeError ("working outside of application/request context") when nothing is pushed.

nodes.label: Request & Response
nodes.summary: Flask's Request and Response classes, extending Werkzeug's with app-config-aware limits and endpoint/blueprint lookups.
nodes.details:
- Request adds url_rule, view_args, routing_exception, and config-driven size limits (max content length, form memory, form parts).
- In debug mode, patches request.files to raise a friendlier error when a form's enctype is wrong.
- Response defaults to text/html and reads max_cookie_size from app config.

nodes.label: Session cookie signing
nodes.summary: Loads and saves the session as a signed cookie, so logins and flashed messages survive between requests.
nodes.details:
- SessionInterface defines open_session/save_session; SecureCookieSessionInterface is the default, signing a JSON payload with ItsDangerous.
- Decides whether to set, refresh, or delete the Set-Cookie header based on whether the session was modified or accessed.
- NullSession is a read-only stand-in used when no secret key is configured.

nodes.label: Context signals
nodes.summary: Blinker signals fired as a context is pushed, popped, or a message is flashed, for extensions to hook into.
nodes.details:
- appcontext_pushed and appcontext_popped fire around AppContext.push()/pop().
- request_started, request_finished, request_tearing_down, got_request_exception, template_rendered, and message_flashed are sent elsewhere in the app using the same namespace.

nodes.label: Request-scoped helpers
nodes.summary: flash(), url_for(), redirect(), abort(), send_file(), and stream_with_context() reach into the active context from a view.
nodes.details:
- flash() and get_flashed_messages() store and retrieve messages in the session, and fire message_flashed.
- url_for(), redirect(), and abort() delegate to the current app so overrides are respected.
- stream_with_context() keeps request/session/g alive for a generator that outlives the normal context.
- send_file()/send_from_directory() pull defaults (root path, max age, send_file settings) from the active app and request.

nodes.label: Debug diagnostics
nodes.summary: Friendlier error messages in debug mode for missing file uploads, bad routing redirects, and template-loader misses.
nodes.details:
- DebugFilesKeyError explains a likely multipart/form-data mistake when request.files is missing an expected key.
- FormDataRoutingRedirect warns when a redirect would silently drop form data on a non-GET request.
- explain_template_loading_attempts() logs every loader tried when a template can't be found.

nodes.label: Error logging
nodes.summary: Sets up the app's logger and picks where error output goes: the WSGI error stream during a request, stderr otherwise.
nodes.details:
- create_logger() configures app.logger, defaulting to DEBUG level when app.debug is on.
- wsgi_errors_stream routes log output to environ['wsgi.errors'] when a request is active, or sys.stderr when it isn't.

flows.name: What happens when a request is handled
flows.summary: A context is pushed before the view runs and popped, with teardown, after the response is sent.

steps.text: Flask builds an AppContext from the WSGI environ and pushes it, setting the active context.
The pushed context becomes what request, session, g, and current_app resolve to.
Pushing opens the session, verifying the signed cookie from the request.
Flask matches the URL against the app's routes while the context is active.
Control returns to the app to dispatch the matched view and build a response.
Push and pop each fire a signal so extensions can hook in.
After the response is ready, the context is popped: teardown functions run, the session is saved to the response, then the context is cleared.

flows.name: What happens when a view calls a context-aware helper
flows.summary: flash(), url_for(), redirect(), and abort() all reach into the active context via the proxies.

steps.text: A view calls flash(), url_for(), redirect(), or abort().
The helper reads the active app and session through the proxies rather than taking them as arguments.
flash() also fires the message_flashed signal.
url_for(), redirect(), and abort() delegate to methods on the Flask app object itself.

flows.name: What happens when something goes wrong in debug mode
flows.summary: Debug mode swaps in richer error objects and messages for template and form mistakes.

steps.text: When form parsing finds no files but the content type isn't multipart, the request flags a likely enctype mistake.
In debug mode, the request patches request.files to raise a descriptive DebugFilesKeyError instead of a plain KeyError.
Template loader failures get a detailed trace of every loader tried, logged for the developer.
Diagnostic messages are written through the app's logger.

nodes.label: Templates and JSON
nodes.summary: Renders Jinja templates and serialises JSON responses, including tagged JSON for session cookies.

nodes.label: Jinja Loader
nodes.summary: Builds Flask's Jinja Environment and finds templates across the app and its blueprints.
nodes.details:
- DispatchingJinjaLoader checks the app's own loader first, then each blueprint's loader in turn.
- EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING switches on verbose lookup logging for debugging missing templates.
- list_templates collects every template name visible app-wide.

nodes.label: Render Functions
nodes.summary: Public render_template/stream_template helpers that fetch a template and render it with the current context.
nodes.details:
- Merges g, request, and user context processors into the template context before rendering.
- Sends before_render_template and template_rendered signals around each render.
- Streaming variants yield chunks instead of returning one string.

nodes.label: JSON Functions
nodes.summary: Module-level dumps/loads/jsonify functions that defer to the active app's JSON provider.
nodes.details:
- Falls back to the stdlib json module when there is no app context.
- jsonify always needs an app context since it builds a Response object.

nodes.label: JSON Provider
nodes.summary: JSONProvider base class and the default implementation that serializes values and builds JSON responses.
nodes.details:
- DefaultJSONProvider handles dates, UUIDs, Decimal, dataclasses, and Markup objects.
- Sorts keys and escapes non-ASCII by default; pretty-prints when the app is in debug mode.
- Apps can swap in a different JSON library by subclassing JSONProvider.

nodes.label: Tagged JSON
nodes.summary: Lossless tag-based serializer used to pack dicts, tuples, bytes, dates, and Markup into session cookies.
nodes.details:
- Each extra type gets a short tag key so it round-trips exactly through plain JSON.
- Extensible: an app can register additional tags for its own types.
- Used as the intermediate serializer before ItsDangerous signs the cookie.

flows.name: What happens when a view renders a template
flows.summary: A view calls render_template; Flask finds the template via the loaders and renders it with signals.

steps.text: View function calls render_template(name, **context)
Asks the environment's loader to find the template source
Merges template context, renders with Jinja, sends before/after signals
Fires the template_rendered signal via Blinker

flows.name: What happens when a view returns JSON
flows.summary: jsonify, or an auto-converted dict/list, goes through the app's JSON provider to build a Response.

steps.text: View returns a dict/list, or calls jsonify() directly
Delegates to current_app.json, the active provider
Serializes with json.dumps and wraps it in a Response with the JSON mimetype

flows.name: What happens when session data is signed into a cookie
flows.summary: Non-JSON session values are tagged for a lossless round trip, then signed by ItsDangerous.

steps.text: The session interface hands the session dict to TaggedJSONSerializer
Tags special types, then dumps the result via flask.json.dumps
ItsDangerous signs the compact JSON string into the cookie

nodes.label: flask command
nodes.summary: The `flask` command line: finds the app, runs the dev server, opens a shell, and hosts custom commands.
nodes.details: `ScriptInfo` locates the app from `--app`, `FLASK_APP`, or a `wsgi.py`/`app.py` in the current folder. `FlaskGroup` builds on Click, and apps and blueprints can attach their own commands.

nodes.label: Test client
nodes.summary: Builds WSGI requests in memory so tests call the app without a server; includes a CLI runner.

nodes.label: Pallets libraries
nodes.summary: Werkzeug (WSGI, routing, request objects), Jinja (templates), Click (CLI), Blinker (signals), ItsDangerous (signing).

nodes.label: Test suite and CI
nodes.summary: Pytest suite covering every module, plus GitHub Actions that run it and publish releases.

nodes.label: Test fixtures
nodes.summary: Pytest fixtures that build a disposable Flask app, request/app contexts, and test client for every test.
nodes.details:
- `app`, `app_ctx`, `req_ctx`, `client` fixtures used by nearly every test module.
- `leak_detector` fails a test if it left an app context pushed.
- `test_apps` and `modules_tmp_path` fixtures juggle `sys.path` for CLI/import tests.

nodes.label: Core behavior tests
nodes.summary: Unit tests for the Flask app object itself: config, contexts, subclassing, signals, and session interfaces.

nodes.label: Blueprint & template tests
nodes.summary: Tests for blueprints, view classes, URL converters, template rendering, JSON, async views, and error handlers.

nodes.label: CLI tests
nodes.summary: Tests for the flask command line, using small sample apps and helper/logging behavior.

nodes.label: Test client tests
nodes.summary: Tests for the test client and request object that other test modules rely on.

nodes.label: Sample Flask apps
nodes.summary: Small sample Flask apps, templates, and static files that other tests load and run against.
nodes.details:
- `test_apps/cliapp`, `blueprintapp`, `helloworld`, `subdomaintestmodule` are miniature apps the CLI and blueprint tests import or invoke.
- `templates/` and `static/` hold Jinja templates and static assets rendered in template/config tests.

nodes.label: Typing checks
nodes.summary: Typing-only fixtures that mypy checks to confirm Flask's public API type hints are sound.

nodes.label: CI test matrix
nodes.summary: GitHub Actions that run the pytest matrix, pre-commit linting, and zizmor's workflow security scan on every PR and push.
nodes.details:
- tests.yaml runs pytest across many Python versions/OSes plus a separate mypy typing job.
- pre-commit.yaml re-runs the repo's lint hooks.
- zizmor.yaml statically scans the workflow files themselves for security issues.

nodes.label: Release workflow
nodes.summary: GitHub Action that builds, drafts a release for, and publishes a tagged version to PyPI.
nodes.details:
- Triggered only by pushing a git tag.
- Builds the package with `uv build`, drafts a GitHub release with the artifacts, then publishes to PyPI using a trusted OIDC token (no stored password).

nodes.label: Issue auto-lock
nodes.summary: Nightly cron job that locks closed issues, PRs, and discussions idle for two weeks.

flows.name: What happens when a developer opens a pull request
flows.summary: A PR or push kicks off the full test, lint, and security-scan matrix before anything merges.

steps.text: Opens a pull request or pushes to main/stable.
GitHub Actions starts the Tests, pre-commit, and zizmor workflows.
Each test run boots fixtures that build a fresh Flask app and client.
Core, web, CLI, and client-test modules exercise their slice of Flask against that app.
A separate job runs mypy over the typing fixtures to check the public API's type hints.

flows.name: What happens when a maintainer pushes a version tag
flows.summary: A tag push builds the package and ships it to PyPI without a maintainer touching credentials.

steps.text: Pushes a git tag such as 3.2.0.
The tag push triggers the Publish workflow.
Builds the package, drafts a GitHub release with the build artifacts, then publishes to PyPI via a trusted OIDC token.

flows.name: What happens every night
flows.summary: A cron job quietly closes the loop on old, inactive issue threads.

steps.text: A daily cron trigger fires at midnight.
Locks closed issues, PRs, and discussions idle for 14+ days, so maintainers don't have to triage them by hand.

nodes.label: Docs and examples
nodes.summary: Sphinx documentation and three runnable example apps: the tutorial blog, a JavaScript demo, and Celery tasks.

nodes.label: Sphinx documentation
nodes.summary: The docs.flask.palletsprojects.com site, built with Sphinx, including the step-by-step tutorial that narrates building the flaskr example.
nodes.details:
- docs/conf.py configures the Pallets Sphinx theme, intersphinx links to Werkzeug/Jinja/Click, and a `:gh:` role linking to source on GitHub.
- docs/tutorial/ is prose that walks a reader through writing each file in the flaskr example, in order.

nodes.label: Tutorial blog (flaskr)
nodes.summary: The flaskr blog app built across the tutorial: user accounts and a list of posts anyone logged in can write.
nodes.details:
- Packaged as its own pip-installable project (pyproject.toml) so the tutorial can demonstrate packaging, not just scripting.
- Uses an application factory plus two blueprints (auth, blog) and a SQLite database.

nodes.label: App factory
nodes.summary: create_app() builds the Flask instance, loads config, ensures the instance folder exists, and wires in the database and blueprints.

nodes.label: Database access
nodes.summary: Opens one SQLite connection per request (stored on `g`), closes it on teardown, and exposes the `flask init-db` CLI command.

nodes.label: Auth blueprint
nodes.summary: Registration, login, and logout views, plus a before-request hook that loads the current user into `g.user`.

nodes.label: Blog blueprint
nodes.summary: Lists, creates, updates, and deletes posts; write actions are guarded by auth's login_required decorator.

nodes.label: Tutorial test suite
nodes.summary: Pytest tests for flaskr covering the factory, the database, and every auth and blog view.
nodes.details:
- conftest.py loads data.sql into a temp SQLite file per test and yields Flask's test client.
- One test module per app module: test_factory, test_db, test_auth, test_blog.

nodes.label: JavaScript demo
nodes.summary: A tiny Flask app with one view that serves three versions of the same form (fetch, XHR, jQuery) that all POST to the same add endpoint.
nodes.details: Demonstrates calling a Flask view from client-side JavaScript without a page reload: the form submits numbers, the view returns JSON, the page updates the result in place.

nodes.label: Celery demo app
nodes.summary: A Flask app whose views submit background jobs and let the browser poll for results, used to document Flask + Celery integration.
nodes.details:
- create_app() builds the Flask instance and calls celery_init_app(), which makes Celery tasks run inside a Flask app context.
- make_celery.py is the entry point the `celery` CLI loads to start a worker against this same app/config.
- views.py exposes POST /tasks/add, /block, /process and GET /tasks/result/<id>.

nodes.label: Celery tasks
nodes.summary: The add/block/process jobs: plain functions decorated with @shared_task so Celery can queue and run them.

nodes.label: Celery worker + Redis
nodes.summary: A separate OS process (`celery -A make_celery worker`) that pulls queued jobs off Redis, runs them, and writes results back.
nodes.details: Redis is used as both the message broker and the result backend (configured in create_app's CELERY mapping). Not part of the Flask WSGI process; started and stopped independently.

flows.name: What happens when a reader works through the tutorial
flows.summary: The docs walk a reader through building flaskr piece by piece, then its own tests verify the result.

steps.text: The tutorial narrates building the flaskr blog app, file by file
Reader follows along writing the factory, database helpers, and the auth/blog blueprints
Each finished feature gets a pytest test exercising it through Flask's test client

flows.name: What happens when a browser submits a background job
flows.summary: A view hands work to Celery instead of doing it inline, and the browser polls for the result.

steps.text: Browser POSTs to /tasks/add, /tasks/block, or /tasks/process
The view calls task.delay(...), queuing the job instead of running it inline
The separately-running Celery worker pulls the job from Redis and executes it inside a Flask app context
Browser polls GET /tasks/result/<id>, which reads the job's status and value back from Redis

flows.name: What happens when a request arrives
flows.summary: One HTTP request, from the server's call to the bytes going back out.

steps.text: The server calls the app object; `__call__` hands off to `wsgi_app` with the WSGI environ.
`wsgi_app` builds a context for the request and pushes it, so `request` and `session` become available and the cookie session is opened.
`before_request` hooks run; if none returns early, the URL is matched and the view function is called.
The view usually renders a template or returns a dict, which becomes JSON.
`make_response` normalises the return value, `after_request` hooks run, the session is saved, and the context is popped with teardown handlers.
The response object is called with `start_response` and its body goes back to the client.

flows.name: Starting an app with `flask run`
flows.summary: How the command line finds an app and serves it.

steps.text: The developer runs `flask --app hello run` (or relies on FLASK_APP or a wsgi.py).
`ScriptInfo` imports the module and finds the app instance or `create_app` factory.
The run command starts Werkzeug's development server with the reloader and debugger as configured.
From then on, every request takes the request path above.

flows.name: Building an application
flows.summary: What the developer's setup code does before any request arrives.

steps.text: `Flask(__name__)` creates the app and works out its root path for templates and static files.
`@app.route` and blueprint registration add URL rules and view functions; blueprints replay their recorded setup onto the app.
Config is loaded from objects, files, or environment variables, and hooks and error handlers are attached.

flows.name: Testing an app without a server
flows.summary: How tests exercise an app in process.

steps.text: A test asks the app for `test_client()` (or `test_cli_runner()`).
The client builds a WSGI environ in memory and calls the app directly, keeping cookies between requests.
The request runs the normal context and dispatch path, so tests see real behaviour.

coverage: Mapped from the repository's contents only. User-level settings, connectors (MCP servers configured outside the repo), scheduled jobs, and secrets usually live outside a repository, so they are not visible here.
